keptItems.title: The MAGA Movement Is Splintering Without Charlie Kirk
keptItems.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. When Charlie Kirk was assassinated last September, many of his allies on the right memorialized him as a hero of free speech and the founder of an enduring political movement. Critics on the left tended to emphasize his long history of offensive remarks and dismiss him as little more than a troll. With a year of distance, neither view appears complete. Since his death, the MAGA movement has stumbled: Its factions are bickering, and Republicans are facing potentially disastrous midterm elections. President Trump seems disconnected from his base and reality. The current plight points to Kirk’s rare ability as a political node, someone who united otherwise disparate forces under one umbrella—and also to how much the movement depended on Kirk personally. Just how fragile a peace Kirk had managed to keep became clear three months after his killing, at an annual conference of Turning Point USA, the organization he’d co-founded. At the summit, feuding parties each tried to claim Kirk’s endorsement of their views. Ben Shapiro, the Daily Wire impresario, used the occasion to blast the broadcaster Tucker Carlson for conducting softball interviews with anti-Semites and other white supremacists. Citing Kirk’s stiff-arming of the Hitler-admiring influencer Nick Fuentes, whose followers were sometimes ejected from Turning Point events, Shapiro assailed Carlson for giving Fuentes a platform. keptItems.title: What Makes Tennis One of the Greatest Games
keptItems.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here. The American tennis player Ben Shelton blasted a 146-mile-an-hour ace past the Spaniard Carlos Alcaraz at 3:33 a.m. yesterday. It was the final shot of a U.S. Open quarterfinal match that had begun 4 hours and 28 minutes before, during which the two men contested five sets, two tiebreakers, and many points so long and improbable that they made the television announcers giggle with delight. When it was done, Shelton and Alcaraz embraced warmly at the net, as if in mutual appreciation for having shared something so grand. The contest, which Shelton afterward described as a “war,” was an emphatic affirmation of a claim made by Arthur Stanwood Pier in The Atlantic 123 years ago : that tennis “is entitled to the place of supremacy among games.” If the case for this assertion is clear today, it was perhaps less obvious in 1903, when the question of which sport should hold such a title was no small matter among men—particularly elite white men—who spent a good deal of time discussing the import of athletics and manliness. Tennis, no matter how much Pier insisted, usually did not rate a mention at all. Far from being only amusements or diversions then, sports were considered serious undertakings that had the job of making men men and rescuing the nation from softness and degeneracy. keptItems.title: What Bush Understood That Trump Doesn’t
keptItems.summaryEvidence: T he current New York City mayor , Zohran Mamdani, has affronted one of his predecessors, Rudy Giuliani, by taking the inflammatory step of deciding to attend the city’s 9/11 commemoration. “It offends me,” Giuliani proclaimed earlier this week on Newsmax. One might suspect that the nature of Mamdani’s offense lay in his being a politician who is associating himself with a day that Giuliani prefers to associate with Giuliani. But the former mayor proceeded to lay out a much darker rationale. “They’re taking over certain parts of America and certain parts of Europe. They have every desire to take us over. This is not ‘they want to be just another religion,’” he said of Muslims. “Mamdani is a clear, a clear supporter of that. All of the Muslims he supports are murderers!” Like many of Giuliani’s utterances, this one has no connection to reality. Yet his assertion that Mamdani harbors some secret desire to conquer the United States in the name of Islam, that his religion is the skeleton key to a web of sinister motivations, is now treated on the right as almost banal. A quarter century after 9/11, delirious anti-Muslim bigotry is almost routine in the political rhetoric of many conservatives. T he conventional account of Donald Trump’s political career explains his rise to power as a populist revolt against Republican orthodoxy. The GOP elite had lost touch with their base by endorsing immigration reform, free trade, or forever wars in the Middle East, which created an opening that Trump exploited. keptItems.title: The Los Angeles Rams Are Trying to Defeat Time
keptItems.summaryEvidence: Usually, when the San Francisco 49ers and the Los Angeles Rams play, it’s a relatively short commute. But this evening, the teams will kick off the NFL’s first-ever regular-season game in Australia. The two teams have taken diametrically opposite approaches to preventing the 8,000-mile journey from disorienting their stars. The 49ers boarded their 16-hour flight to Melbourne nine days ago and have spent the intervening time training, watching Aussie rules football, and winning the majority of local support. The Rams landed yesterday, just 24 hours before the game. They’re betting on being in Australia so briefly that players’ brains and bodies won’t notice the difference. That makes the game the most high-profile test of jet-lag-evasion techniques in American sports history. Anyone who has hurled across several time zones in one go knows how wide-awake and helplessly sleepy you can feel at inappropriate hours upon landing—a major inconvenience for professional football players, whose career depends on how they perform during one very specific period. Circadian rhythms can also affect performance in less obvious ways. Compounds that encourage inflammation, for instance, spike at night, when the body is doing less and can direct more energy toward fighting infection. A new time zone throws that optimal function off tilt and can cause stomach issues, cognitive impairment, headaches, and mood changes. Teams at a circadian disadvantage tend to play worse. keptItems.summaryEvidence: S ecretary of State Colin Powell was having breakfast with Peru’s president in Lima’s historic center on September 11, 2001, when an aide passed him a note to inform him that a plane had struck the World Trade Center. Minutes later, he received a second note. “Oh my God,” Powell said aloud. keptItems.title: The Thrill of Wanting AI to Destroy the World
keptItems.summaryEvidence: T he sky streaked orange and red as my mother drove us home to Albuquerque through the Tijeras Pass, which separates the Sandia Mountains to the north from the Manzanos to the south. “Look out for mushroom clouds,” my father said to her. “If you see them, turn around.” He did this every time we returned to town from the rugged canyon to the east, but the sunsets always egged him on. According to legend, a part of the Manzanos, whose foothills descend into Kirtland Air Force Base and then Sandia National Laboratories, had been hollowed out to hold live nuclear warheads. My father insisted that, in the event of a nuclear attack, Albuquerque was slated to receive two bombs from the sky, one each for these secret government sites. He delivered this information as if it were a law of physics or the known terms of an international treaty. I was a child, so I took it as such, staring bug-eyed at the red sky that might evaporate me. Nearly two decades later, I looked up at the clear blue one above Los Angeles from behind the wheel of my own car, worried about different missiles. I had gone into my dot-com job early, and I was the only one there when the planes hit the Twin Towers. The internet, barely functional on a good day, broke completely; to listen to the news, I had to turn on a transistor radio that someone had left in their cubicle. We sent everyone home early that morning. I recalled an article published a handful of years earlier, just before the stark-white, cliffside Getty Center opened in Brentwood. keptItems.title: What the Failure to Convict the Alleged 9/11 Mastermind Reveals
keptItems.summaryEvidence: Prosecutors trying to finally convict Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged mastermind of the September 11 attacks, got some good news and some bad news last month. The good news is that a judge set a date for Mohammed’s trial in a military court. The bad news is that the trial won’t begin until June 2028—oh, and the judge also threw out a confession Mohammed made in 2007. The problem is how the U.S. government obtained the confession. Mohammed was captured on March 1, 2003, in Pakistan. He was then held in a series of secret CIA “black sites,” allegedly including spots in Afghanistan, Jordan, Poland, and Romania, before being brought to the U.S. prison at Guantánamo Bay in 2006. Throughout his imprisonment, he was subject to what U.S. officials called “enhanced interrogation techniques”—or, in plain English, torture. Lieutenant Colonel Michael Schrama, the judge, reportedly concluded that “the prosecution has failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Mr. Mohammad’s statements to the F.B.I. were voluntarily given.” A quarter century has passed since the attacks, long enough that Americans born after 9/11 are themselves adults—some have even died in conflicts that are part of the war on terror. The failure to convict Mohammed by now is an open wound and an embarrassment, one that shows how the government cutting corners and breaking rules can actually end up making the pursuit of justice harder and slower.
